chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Monk, Klook Clarke and Minton's, and the first bop records
summary: The Minton's house band, wire recordings, Hawkins's 'Woody'n You' and Dizzy's small-group sides.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Now, Klook Clarke was in this band at Minton's Playhouse. The band consisted of Monk on piano, Kermit Scott, tenor player, that's up in San Francisco now, Joe Guy on trumpet, Kenny Clarke on drums, and a bass player named Nick Penton. Now, Monk and Klook Clarke, they cooperated on these chords, because you see, Kenny Clarke, who was known as Klook Clarke, could play vibes, but he didn't have any vibes, you know. He had some bells. A little, small, compact thing, that he played bells occasionally. But he could pick out some changes and things on these bells, you know. And together they got this thing together. So Diz got it in a hurry. Charlie Christian was coming down and sitting in. A fellow named Jerry Newton was taking all of these jam sessions off on wire tape. They didn't have tape recorders at that time. They had wire tape. And some of them are floating around now, commercially. You know, Minton's Playhouse jam sessions. Charlie Christian, Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker on them. And the first person to record be-bop was Coleman Hawkins. He had Dizzy in the band and he recorded 'Woody'n You'. That was one of the first be-bop tunes recorded. But it didn't go over. It didn't sell. Now, Diz, when he recorded it, he cleaned it up and put his own arrangements in, after he had learned the charts and everything. He arranged his own music.
* Jerry Newman. No, Dick Hecker - wire tape

And he had been arranging all along for Woody Herman for awhile, you know. So he comes out and he records "Hot House" and "Salted Peanuts", with a small combo. He and Charlie Parker and Al Haig, Stan Levy, Milt Jackson -- no, no, Milt wasn't on that session. And Ray Brown. "Hot House", "Salted Peanuts". I forget the other two.
